Space Zero: Open Ground

Meeting the Future

AI · Care · Creativity · Kathmandu & Lumbini · Oct 28–Nov 4

A gathering of researchers, practitioners, and builders, meeting in Nepal to show each other how we actually work, and to ask what intelligent systems owe to the beings they touch.

In collaboration with the Center for the Study of Apparent Selves (CSAS) · Shedrub Mandala / Gomde California

01

The invitation

This is Open Ground practiced at distance: local attunement carried to a global exchange.

“We are not here to present. We are here to see, and to be seen, in the act of doing what we love.”

The thread connecting us is a question Open Ground already asks at home: what does a place shape in the intelligence that emerges from it, and where do frontier technologies and ancient wisdom actually touch? In Nepal we take that question to ground that has held one of humanity's most sophisticated sciences of mind for two thousand years.

We arrive from AI research, Buddhist philosophy, cognitive science, biology, and contemplative practice, each carrying a different instrument, each mapping the same territory. Sessions are open dialogues, not presentations: each participant offers a window into their work, the room responds, connections form.

Care, in the framework of CSAS and the work of Dr. Michael Levin (Tufts University), is not sentiment but a functional driver of intelligence across every scale of life: cellular, communal, artificial. Buddhist philosophy has held a version of this for two millennia in the figure of the bodhisattva, an intelligence that takes the welfare of others as its operating instruction.

02

Why Nepal, why now

The choice of coordinate system changes what you can see.

Lumbini is the ground where the historical Buddha is said to have declared his intention to liberate beings from suffering. It is a fitting place to ask what we owe the minds we are building, and it triangulates a question Space Zero: Open Ground can't fully answer from Crescent City alone: two independent instruments, ancient contemplative science and frontier AI research, locating something neither could find on its own.

Season arc

This gathering follows directly from Space Zero's own season: The Emergent exhibition gathers in Crescent City October 3–5, closing a year of Lab Zero residencies. Three and a half weeks later, Open Ground carries that same inquiry into a wider, older field of practice: benevolent emergence, care as a driver of intelligence.

03

The journey

Eight days: four in Kathmandu, four in Lumbini. Stay on for the full ten-day recitation if you wish.

Dates
October 28 – November 4, 2026
Where
Kathmandu & Lumbini, Nepal
Who
~10–20 researchers & practitioners
Format
In-person, with online participation available
Logistics
Flights, transfers & hotel bookings handled by the organizing team
Kathmandu · 4 days
Day 1Oct 28

Arrival

Check-in at Hyatt Regency Kathmandu, steps from Boudhanath Stupa. Evening orientation, first dinner together.

Day 2Oct 29

Boudhanath & Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling

A walking tour of Boudhanath led by Jack deTar: circumambulation of the stupa, a visit to Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling Monastery, with a possible audience with Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche.

Day 3Oct 30

Pharping & Asura Cave

Pilgrimage to the cave where Padmasambhava is said to have attained realization. Time for reflection in a landscape shaped by centuries of practice.

Day 4Oct 31

Departure to Lumbini

Morning at leisure; afternoon flight to Lumbini, birthplace of the historical Buddha.

Lumbini · 4 days
Days 5–8Nov 1–4

Recitation, dialogue, teaching

Mornings at the Annual Recitation of the Buddha's Words; late morning dialogue sessions in the temple complex on AI, alignment, and ethics; afternoons of teaching and meditation instruction from Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche and Phakchok Rinpoche; evenings of unstructured conversation over dinner, where much of the real work happens.

04

Who's gathering

Researchers and practitioners spanning AI alignment, Buddhist philosophy, biology, and contemplative science.

Adam Goldstein

Co-founder of Softmax; formerly of Dr. Michael Levin's lab at Tufts, studying bioelectricity and basal cognition. Architect of “organic alignment,” the thesis that principles governing alignment in ant colonies and cellular organisms apply equally to AI systems.

Bill Duane

Strategy and Implementation Lead at CSAS; former engineering executive at Google and Google's first Superintendent of Wellbeing. Teaches at Stanford's d.school; Research Fellow at Kathmandu University.

Dr. Thomas Doctor

Professor of Buddhist Studies at Kathmandu University; AI Strategic Consultant to 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha.
